sentences.text: Quinkana is distinguished by a unique combination of ziphodont teeth and a deep, altirostral skull. These ziphodont teeth were recurved, serrated, and blade-like, designed for cutting flesh.
Although the genus is known for these specialized teeth, the holotype of Q. fortirostrum did not preserve teeth in their sockets, so this feature is inferred from other specimens.
The animal is typically estimated to be about 3 meters long and weigh around 200 kilograms.
The genus Quinkana was described by Molnar in 1981, with the type species being Quinkana fortirostrum.
Charles Walter De Vis found early Quinkana fossils in the Darling Downs region of Queensland in 1886.
Later, Lyndsey Hawkins discovered significant Quinkana fossil material in the Tea Tree Cave in 1970.

Ralph Molnar cautiously proposed that Quinkana was a terrestrial predator based on its cranial anatomy, though he acknowledged counterarguments to this idea. The proportions of the snout and specialized dentition of Quinkana are often cited as evidence for a terrestrial lifestyle.

During the Pleistocene, Quinkana was one of the large terrestrial predators of Australia. Q. fortirostrum was one of the largest predators in Australia of its time, surpassed only in size by the giant monitor Megalania.
Four species are currently recognized within the genus Quinkana: Q. fortirostrum, Q. timara, Q. babarra, and Q. meboldi.
In 1993, various Australasian fossil crocodilian species, including those of Quinkana, were placed in the subfamily Mekosuchinae.

Quinkana lived in Australia from approximately 25 million years ago until about 20,000 years ago. It survived the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene arid period but went extinct at the end of the Pleistocene.
Specifically, Quinkana timara lived during the middle to late Miocene in the Northern Territory of Australia.
Other estimates suggest the genus lived in Australia from about 24 million years ago until about 40,000 years ago.

Paleontologists debate whether Quinkana was terrestrial or semi-aquatic. The ecological role of Quinkana in Late Pleistocene Australia is debated. It is hypothesized that intense aridification caused Quinkana's extinction by drying river basins and destroying forests. There is ongoing debate regarding Quinkana's role in prehistoric Australian ecosystems and whether it was terrestrial.
